newsitem.title: USA: Legendary director Fred Zinnemann dies at 89.
newsitem.headline: Legendary director Fred Zinnemann dies at 89.

text.p: Academy Award-winning director Fred Zinnemann, whose classic films included "High Noon," "From Here to Eternity" and "A Man for All Seasons," died on Friday at 89, the Los Angeles Times said on Saturday.
The newspaper said that Zinnemann's death in London, where he had lived for more than 30 years, was disclosed by his son, Tim, a producer in Los Angeles. The precise cause of death was not given.
The director earned Oscars for directing the feature film "From Here to Eternity" in 1953, and two more Oscars for directing and producing "A Man for All Seasons" in 1966.
Five of his films -- "The Search," "High Noon," "From Here to Eternity," "A Man for All Seasons" and "Julia" -- collected a total of 25 Academy Awards.
During his 40-year career Zinnemann made about 20 films and worked with such top stars as Gary Cooper and Audrey Hepburn. He introduced Marlon Brando to filmgoers in "The Men" in 1950.
He also directed the musical "Oklahoma," the "The Nun's Story" and the classic thriller "The Day of the Jackal."
Known as a master craftsman, Zinnemann was able to rally colleagues to match his high professional standards and to make serious films that were box office successes, the Los Angeles Times said.

He largely stopped making films after "Five Days One Summer" with Sean Connery in 1982 partly because of age and health problems and partly because he was dispirited by the venemous reviews the film received.

That Hollywood did respect his output was evident in his number of Oscars and a special award from the Academy of Motion Picure Arts and Sciences when he dedicated his personal library to the organisation.
Born in Vienna, Zinnemann started out to become a violinist but abandoned a career in music when he decided he had no talent. He next studied law, earning a degree at the University of Vienna.

But he was impressed by film while a student and in 1927 went to Paris as one of the first students of the Ecole Tehnique de Cinema, where he started by learning optics, photochemistry, development and printing, and worked as an assistant camerman.

He first tackled Hollywood in 1929 as an extra in "All Quiet on the Western Front." He worked his way up from film cutter to an assistant to directors Berthold Viertol, Robert Flaherty and Busby Berkeley.
